subject: Application - (Senior) Site Reliability Engineer, STACKIT Control Plane (GT2321)
paragraphs: I am applying for the (Senior) Site Reliability Engineer role on the STACKIT Control Plane. The posting is unusually precise about what the job is: shorten time-to-detect with monitoring and alerting that holds against defined SLOs, shorten time-to-mitigate with playbooks and telemetry a first responder can actually use, and carry a compensated on-call rotation. That is the work I have been doing alone, on a small estate, for four years, and the appeal of this role is doing it with a control plane's stakes and a team to be accountable with.

Alerting that is derived from recorded state rather than from a green check is the habit I would bring first. A sentinel writes job status, generation age, disk pressure and pressure-stall figures every fifteen minutes into a ledger; gatus pages on any state that is not ok; and a finished socket is explicitly not accepted as a finished job, because the ledger is what settles it. Where I have fallen short of a real SRE practice is scale and SLO discipline: my alerts are thresholds on a single estate, not error-budget policy on a multi-tenant service, and turning indicator thresholds into SLOs with burn-rate alerts is one of the things I want to learn here rather than claim now.

Distributed reliability is where my distance from this role is greatest, so I will be plain about it: I have not operated the Kubernetes control plane — not the API server, the controller manager, the scheduler or etcd — in production, and distributed consensus tuning at that layer is reading, not experience. What I have built is an equivalent reconciliation loop with different tools: one flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts from feature lists, the option surface is derived rather than copied, and the same module gate runs in CI and on the machines. The reasoning about declared state, drift, and a change that must be provable after the fact transfers; the internals of etcd do not.

Linux and secrets are the two areas where the depth is real. Host configuration is code with pinned inputs and hermetic builds, kernel-adjacent symptoms get diagnosed from pressure-stall and disk figures rather than from guesses, and networking decisions are made in nftables tables that default to deny. Access is short-lived by construction: an SSH certificate authority issues certificates with a lifetime rather than leaving keys on hosts, secrets are encrypted per host with SOPS and age so nothing sensitive sits readable in the repository, and patching is ordered by CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and exposure. Zero standing credentials is the design goal, and the certificate authority is how far I have got toward it.

Go is the language I write services in: bountystash is a single-binary Go service with append-only events, content-addressed specifications, a terminal UI and HTTP endpoints, built and operated end to end. PostgreSQL is in production — versioned migrations, a rehearsed restore, statement timeouts, disk-pressure alerting — though as one instance rather than a fleet; Redis, Kafka, NATS, Operators, CNI, eBPF and canary or blue/green delivery at platform scale are all absent from my tool history, because Nix and a task interface occupy those roles here. On languages: English is native and German is C1, so a German-speaking team and an English-speaking one are both workable. On place: I am in south-west Germany, some 230 km from Bad Friedrichshall, and would want to agree the on-site cadence and the on-call arrangement before we go further. I am a US citizen with German permanent residence and need no sponsorship.
